newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Greek PM calls for pressure on Turkey over Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM calls for pressure on Turkey over Cyprus.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis on Wednesday accused Turkey of showing intransigence on the protracted Cyprus dispute and called for international pressure on Ankara to force it to change its course.

Simitis made the call shortly before he left the divided eastern Mediterranean island, winding up a two-day visit for independence day celebrations. Turkey has occupied the northern part of Cyprus since 1974 when it invaded in the wake of a short-lived Greek Cypriot coup inspired by the military regime ruling Greece at the time.

"It is necessary for Ankara to move from its intransigent positions," said Simitis. "If the international community wants progress on the Cyprus problem, it should at least turn to Ankara and demand its compliance to rules of international law and decisions of the United Nations," the Greek premier added.

Earlier on Wednesday, the two governments said they were committed to a peaceful solution to the decades-old division but said any further military advance of Turkey in the island would be a cause of war.
A joint communique released after a Simitis-Clerides meeting said acceptance by Turkey of Clerides's proposal for demilitarisation could ensure "peace and stability in Cyprus and the region."

"It was once again made clear that a further advance of Turkey in Cyprus is a cause of war. Demilitarisation of Cyprus can ensure peace and stability on the island and the region," Cypriot government spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides said.
Greece has a defence pact with Cyprus, whereby Athens will come to Cyprus's aid in the event of any Turkish advance further south in Cyprus.
Turkey maintains some 30,000 troops in the north of Cyprus, declared a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 but recognised only by Ankara.
Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides said Simitis's visit further strengthened cooperation between the two governments on ways to promote the Cyprus issue.
"Today's meeting showed beyond a shadow of doubt that there is a conjunction of views and cooperation between the two governments on handling the Cyprus problem in the future," Clerides said.

Clerides and Simitis reaffirmed the Greek Cypriot side's position that it will attend direct negotiations with the Turkish Cypriot side only if common ground is found on basic issues -- such as sovereignty, territory, guarantees and demilitarisation of the island.
Simitis said Cyprus and Greece would continue to search for a solution through the United Nations but added initiatives from other countries were also welcome.

The protracted dispute has drawn a small army of mediators from the United Nations and other interested countries, but no one has been able to find mutually acceptable terms for the island's reunification as a bicommunal bizonal federation.
Shortly before the meeting started, Clerides awarded Simitis with the Archbishop Makarios III Cross, the highest distinction of the state.
Hundreds of people cheered Simitis at Nicosia town hall at noon where during a ceremony he was made honourary citizen of the capital and given the golden key to the city.
